name: Agriculture
blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

points.desc: Deere's precision agriculture line (See and Spray, autonomous tractors) is the reference commercial deployment.
points.name: Precision ag is shipping product

points.desc: Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its fortnightly AI-use series.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Economic Research Service publishes the data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms - variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, autonomous equipment. The federal measurement layer.
points.name: USDA ERS measures US adoption

points.desc: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact.
points.name: FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally

points.desc: The AgriFoodTech investment research tracks venture capital into agricultural AI, robotics, computer vision, and farm-management software - the sector's funding barometer.
points.name: AgFunder indexes the investment flow

points.desc: Planet Labs' high-resolution imagery, Descartes Labs' geospatial ML, and EarthDaily's field-level crop indicators supply the AI-ready observation data behind yield prediction and crop-stress detection.
points.name: The satellite layer feeds the models

points.desc: The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards, and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production.
points.name: AEM tracks the machinery standards

points.desc: The nonprofit consortium sets the open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites - the plumbing under everything else.
points.name: AgGateway makes the data interoperable

points.desc: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is the scientific organization connecting academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice.
points.name: ISPA bridges the science and the field

points.desc: The 100 Million Farmers initiative tracks AI adoption through the lens of climate-smart and regenerative agriculture metrics globally.
points.name: WEF tracks climate-smart adoption

points.desc: Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular are the large digital-farming platforms turning soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning.
points.name: The agribusiness platforms run the prescriptions

points.desc: CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning, and precision application - the equipment layer beyond Deere.
points.name: CNH and Raven automate the other fleets

points.desc: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide; Monarch builds electric driverless tractors - narrow AI shipping as farm equipment.
points.name: The pure-plays attack single problems

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey recorded agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting at 13.7% AI use in its prior measurement period, with the most recent figure suppressed, making that earlier reading the best available official benchmark for how many firms in the sector reported actively deploying AI. The number is a floor rather than a ceiling, since the survey captures only a fortnightly snapshot and the sector spans operations of vastly different scale and technical capacity.

Where AI is shipping as actual product, the deployments tend to concentrate on three problems: weed control, planting prescriptions, and field monitoring. Carbon Robotics describes its LaserWeeder as powered by a Large Plant Model trained on what it calls the world's largest and most diverse agricultural dataset, collected by machines operating in the field, and it positions the system as physical AI that eliminates weeds without herbicide while letting operators switch between manual and autonomous control. Climate FieldView, the digital farming platform, reports that farmers using its seed scripts saw an average increase of plus five bushels per acre compared with users who wrote their own scripts, which is one of the more concrete ROI figures available from a platform at commercial scale.

On the investment side, AgFunder tracks venture and growth capital flowing into agrifoodtech and reports that global agrifoodtech funding reached approximately 16 billion dollars in 2024, a 4% drop from 2023, with signs of selective recovery. Its 2025 figure stands at 16.2 billion dollars, nearly flat versus the prior year at negative 3%, though AgFunder notes investors are writing checks more selectively and directing capital toward companies with tangible science and clear paths to revenue. Developing markets showed a markedly different trajectory, with funding in those regions growing 63% between 2023 and 2024, and Asia-Pacific agrifoodtech startups raising 4.2 billion dollars through October 2024, a 38% increase over the same period in 2023.

The data infrastructure underpinning AI models in this sector depends on several distinct layers working together. Planet Labs supplies high-frequency, high-resolution satellite imagery that feeds crop monitoring and yield-prediction pipelines, offering what it describes as a global, daily view of Earth's surface. AgGateway, a nonprofit consortium, works on the data-standards plumbing that allows feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites to be ingested by AI systems in interoperable formats, including traceability work spanning grain provenance in North America and farm and cropfield identification standards in Europe. The International Society of Precision Agriculture connects academic remote-sensing and spatial-analytics research to commercial practice, while the Association of Equipment Manufacturers works across autonomous machinery standards and policy for the equipment layer.

The FAO's digital agriculture program has engaged with AI adoption benchmarking, including through the Innovate Africa Challenge launched with Smart Africa to accelerate AI solutions for agricultural and climate challenges on the continent, though African agrifoodtech funding remains a small share of global flows, at 1.6% of the total in the first half of 2024 according to AgFunder. USDA's Economic Research Service maintains the federal measurement layer for precision-agriculture adoption across US farms, covering variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, and autonomous equipment, though the excerpts available from that source do not report a specific current adoption percentage beyond what the Census survey captures.

A decision-maker evaluating whether to deploy AI in this sector should note that the commercial deployments with the clearest evidence are narrow and task-specific, weed identification and laser treatment, seed-script optimization, and satellite-based field monitoring, rather than broad farm management automation. Investment is recovering but investors are explicitly more selective than in earlier years, favoring demonstrated unit economics. The data-interoperability gap, addressed by organizations like AgGateway, remains a practical constraint: AI models are only as useful as the standardized, machine-readable data flowing into them from equipment and sensors, and that infrastructure is still being built out across much of global agriculture.
